subject: Climate & Environment
title: Green Hydrogen
description: A short lesson to help you apply Green Hydrogen.

hook.text: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. It burns clean — just water vapor.

buildup.text: Electrolyzers split water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity.

discovery.text: When that electricity comes from renewables, the hydrogen is completely carbon-free.

twist.text: Right now 96% of hydrogen is made from fossil fuels. Truly green hydrogen barely exists.

climax.text: Costs are dropping fast. Green hydrogen could decarbonize steel, shipping, and aviation.

punchline.text: The cleanest fuel is water, split apart and put back together.

details.summary: Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water with an electrolyzer powered by renewable electricity. It emits no carbon during production or use and could decarbonize sectors like steelmaking, chemicals, and long-haul transport that are difficult to electrify directly.
details.whyItMatters: Green hydrogen is seen as a missing piece of the decarbonization puzzle. It can store renewable energy and fuel industrial processes that batteries cannot easily serve.
takeaways: Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity
Green hydrogen produces zero carbon emissions
It targets hard-to-electrify sectors like steel and shipping

faq.question: Why is most hydrogen today not green?
faq.answer: Over 95 percent of hydrogen is produced from natural gas through steam methane reforming, which emits large amounts of CO2. This gray hydrogen is much cheaper than green hydrogen because renewable electricity and electrolyzers remain more expensive.

faq.question: When will green hydrogen become cost competitive?
faq.answer: Analysts project green hydrogen could match gray hydrogen costs by 2030 in regions with cheap renewables. Falling electrolyzer costs, scaling production, and carbon pricing are the key factors driving competitiveness.
